title: 1 Chronicles 21:9–17
context: Through the prophet Gad, the LORD offers David three judgments; David chooses to fall into the LORD’s hand. Seventy thousand die, and the LORD stops the destroying angel at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. David and the elders, in sackcloth, fall on their faces, and David asks that the punishment fall on him and his father’s house. The parallel in 2 Samuel 24:10-17 offers seven years of famine where 21:12 has three, calls the landowner Araunah, and does not describe the angel standing between earth and sky or the elders in sackcloth.

verses.text: The LORD spoke to Gad, David’s seer, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD speaks to Gad, David’s seer. Arminian readers observe that God answers David’s confession through a prophet he had long known (1 Samuel 22:5), so that the response comes through a familiar and trusted voice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s word governing even the consequences of sin. The seer does not invent the options; he carries a message, and both traditions treat his role as shared ground.

verses.text: “Go and speak to David, saying, ‘The LORD says, “I offer you three things. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: God offers David three things and lets him choose. Arminian readers see God treating David as a responsible agent even in judgment, involving him in the shape of the consequence rather than simply imposing it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God sets the options while giving David a real choice among them. The choice is genuine, yet it lies within limits God has appointed, a pattern both traditions recognize.

verses.text: So Gad came to David and said to him, “The LORD says, ‘Take your choice:
verses.arminianNotes: Gad comes to David with the words, Take your choice. Arminian readers see in the brief, direct message a reminder that God’s dealings with David remain personal even when the news is hard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the prophet’s obedience is immediate and exact. The messenger faithfully delivers what he received, a quiet model of prophetic service that both traditions honor.

verses.text: either three years of famine; or three months to be consumed before your foes, while the sword of your enemies overtakes you; or else three days of the sword of the LORD, even pestilence in the land, and the LORD’s angel destroying throughout all the borders of Israel. Now therefore consider what answer I shall return to him who sent me.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The choices are three years of famine, three months of defeat, or three days of the sword of the LORD. Arminian readers note that 2 Samuel 24:13 has seven years of famine, and they leave the number difference unresolved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also name the difference between the three years here and the seven years in 2 Samuel 24:13. They note that Chronicles describes the pestilence vividly as the LORD’s angel destroying throughout Israel, preparing for the scene that follows.

verses.text: David said to Gad, “I am in distress. Let me fall, I pray, into the LORD’s hand, for his mercies are very great. Don’t let me fall into man’s hand.”
verses.arminianNotes: David says he is in distress and asks to fall into the LORD’s hand, for his mercies are very great. Arminian readers see trust in God’s character as the wise response to deserved judgment, preferring his mercy to human cruelty.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see faith that God’s mercy exceeds man’s, even when God is the one who strikes (Psalm 103:8-14). David’s choice expresses confidence in the character of the God he has offended.

verses.text: So the LORD sent a pestilence on Israel, and seventy thousand men of Israel fell.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD sent a pestilence, and seventy thousand men fell. Arminian readers treat the deaths soberly, as in 2 Samuel 24:15, and they refrain from speculating beyond what the text says about those who died.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the verse with the same sobriety, seeing God’s judgment fall on Israel. The number matches Samuel’s account, and both traditions grieve the loss while affirming that God is just.

verses.text: God sent an angel to Jerusalem to destroy it. As he was about to destroy, the LORD saw, and he relented of the disaster, and said to the destroying angel, “It is enough. Now withdraw your hand.” the LORD’s angel was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
verses.arminianNotes: As the angel is about to destroy Jerusalem, the LORD relents and says, It is enough. Arminian readers see real responsiveness and mercy in God, consistent with the reading given at 2 Samuel 24:16.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read relented as God turning from disaster within his settled purpose. Neither tradition takes it as a change in God’s knowledge or character, as the Samuel notes also say. Here the landowner is named Ornan; 2 Samuel 24:16 calls him Araunah.

verses.text: David lifted up his eyes, and saw the LORD’s angel standing between earth and the sky, having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces.
verses.arminianNotes: David sees the LORD’s angel between earth and sky with a drawn sword over Jerusalem, and he and the elders fall on their faces in sackcloth. Arminian readers see the leaders sharing in public repentance as the nation’s representatives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this vivid scene of the angel and the elders in sackcloth appears only in Chronicles. The sight of the sword makes the danger visible, and humility before God becomes the only fitting posture.

verses.text: David said to God, “Isn’t it I who commanded the people to be counted? It is even I who have sinned and done very wickedly; but these sheep, what have they done? Please let your hand, O LORD my God, be against me and against my father’s house; but not against your people, that they should be plagued.”
verses.arminianNotes: David asks, Isn’t it I who commanded the people to be counted? Arminian readers see a king who accepts full responsibility and asks to bear the judgment himself, interceding like a shepherd for his flock.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the guilt placed squarely on David, consistent with the Samuel notes. Many Christians read his plea, these sheep, what have they done, as pointing ahead to Christ the good shepherd (John 10:11), offered as a reading.
